**Answer: Yes, the fractional $p$-Laplace operator $(-\Delta_p)^s$ is rotationally invariant under orthogonal maps.**

---

**Proof.**

Let $0 < s < 1 < p < \infty$ and $n \geq 1$. The fractional $p$-Laplacian of a sufficiently smooth function $u : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined (up to a positive normalizing constant $C_{n,s,p}$) by the principal value integral

$$(-\Delta_p)^s u(x) = C_{n,s,p}\,\text{P.V.}\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \frac{|u(x)-u(y)|^{p-2}\bigl(u(x)-u(y)\bigr)}{|x-y|^{n+sp}}\,dy.$$

We must show that for every orthogonal map $R \in O(n)$ and every admissible $u$,

$$(-\Delta_p)^s (u \circ R)(x) = \bigl((-\Delta_p)^s u\bigr)(Rx) \qquad \text{for all } x \in \mathbb{R}^n.$$

---

**Step 1: Set up the composition.** Let $v(x) = u(Rx)$. Then

$$(-\Delta_p)^s v(x) = C_{n,s,p}\,\text{P.V.}\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \frac{|v(x)-v(y)|^{p-2}\bigl(v(x)-v(y)\bigr)}{|x-y|^{n+sp}}\,dy.$$

Substituting the definition of $v$:

$$(-\Delta_p)^s v(x) = C_{n,s,p}\,\text{P.V.}\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \frac{|u(Rx)-u(Ry)|^{p-2}\bigl(u(Rx)-u(Ry)\bigr)}{|x-y|^{n+sp}}\,dy.$$

---

**Step 2: Change of variables.** Perform the substitution $z = Ry$. Since $R \in O(n)$:

- **Jacobian:** $|\det R| = 1$, so $dy = dz$.
- **Distance preservation:** $|x - y| = |R(x-y)| = |Rx - Ry| = |Rx - z|$, using orthogonality ($|R\xi| = |\xi|$ for all $\xi$).
- **Domain:** $R$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{R}^n$, so the range of integration is unchanged.

Under this substitution the integrand becomes

$$\frac{|u(Rx)-u(z)|^{p-2}\bigl(u(Rx)-u(z)\bigr)}{|Rx-z|^{n+sp}},$$

and therefore

$$(-\Delta_p)^s v(x) = C_{n,s,p}\,\text{P.V.}\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \frac{|u(Rx)-u(z)|^{p-2}\bigl(u(Rx)-u(z)\bigr)}{|Rx-z|^{n+sp}}\,dz.$$

---

**Step 3: Identify the result.** The right-hand side is exactly the definition of $(-\Delta_p)^s u$ evaluated at the point $Rx$:

$$(-\Delta_p)^s v(x) = \bigl((-\Delta_p)^s u\bigr)(Rx).$$

Recalling $v = u \circ R$, we conclude

$$\boxed{(-\Delta_p)^s (u \circ R)(x) = \bigl((-\Delta_p)^s u\bigr)(Rx) \qquad \forall\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n,\ \forall\, R \in O(n).}$$

---

**Why the proof works — the two structural ingredients:**

1. **Isotropic kernel.** The singular kernel $|x-y|^{-(n+sp)}$ depends only on the Euclidean distance $|x-y|$. Orthogonal maps preserve distances, so the kernel is invariant under $x \mapsto Rx,\; y \mapsto Ry$.

2. **Pointwise nonlinearity.** The factor $|u(x)-u(y)|^{p-2}(u(x)-u(y))$ is a *scalar* function of the scalar difference $u(x)-u(y)$; it involves no derivatives or geometric structure that could break symmetry. Under composition $v = u \circ R$ it simply becomes $|u(Rx)-u(Ry)|^{p-2}(u(Rx)-u(Ry))$, which after the change of variables $z = Ry$ is exactly the same expression appearing in $(-\Delta_p)^s u$ at the point $Rx$.

These two facts together — combined with $|\det R| = 1$ so the volume element is preserved — yield rotational invariance. The argument places no restriction on $p > 1$ (the case $p = 2$ recovers the classical fractional Laplacian, well known to be rotationally invariant), so the conclusion holds for the full range $0 < s < 1 < p < \infty$.
